column1: Does Trump’s Tariff Make America Great Again? An Empirical Analysis of US–China Trade War Impact on American Business Formation (2018–2025)

The thesis titled An Empirical Analysis of Tiff's Impact on American Business Formation by Ruiming Min investigates the effects of tariff policies  particularly those stemming from the US-China trade war initiated in 2018  on American business formation. The study uses county-level business application data from 2018 to 2025 to analyze the relationship between tariff implementation and new business formation through linear regression analysis. The findings reveal a statistically significant positive association between US tariffs on China and American business applications. However  when Chinese retaliatory tariffs are included in the analysis  their negative coefficient substantially exceeds the positive US tariff effect  suggesting that retaliatory measures largely offset the benefits of protectionist policies. Control variables such as inflation rate  federal funds rate  and government spending show significant positive effects on business formation. These results indicate that while protectionist trade policies may stimulate domestic business formation  their effectiveness is significantly diminished by retaliatory responses from trading partners. The study provides evidence that unilateral tariff measures without diplomatic coordination produce limited net benefits  confirming that trade wars create scenarios where potential gains are neutralized by counteractions.

The introduction of the thesis discusses the political context of the US-China trade war  initiated under President Donald Trump's administration with the promise of revitalizing American manufacturing and creating jobs. Previous research  such as that by Fajgelbaum et al. (2020) and Amiti et al. (2019)  has shown that tariffs led to significant declines in imports and exports  with complete pass-through of tariffs to US consumers. However  this study finds evidence that contradicts the wholly negative assessments by analyzing the relationship between tariff policies and business application rates in the United States  suggesting that tariffs may have stimulated new business formation.

The data and methods section outlines the study's focus on data from 2018 to 2025  covering the full evolution of the trade war. The study uses business application data from the US Census Bureau and tariff data from the Peterson Institute for International Economics. Control variables include the unemployment rate  inflation rate  federal funds rate  and government spending. The study employs a linear regression model to analyze the data  with the US tariffs on China as the primary independent variable of interest.

The results and discussion section presents the regression results  showing significant relationships between US tariff increases and business formation. Without considering Chinese tariffs  a one percentage point increase in US tariffs on China is associated with a significant increase in business applications. However  when Chinese tariffs are included  the positive effect of US tariffs is offset by the negative impact of Chinese retaliatory tariffs. The study concludes that while Trump's tariffs had a positive effect on the return of American firms  the counterattacks by China and other countries offset this positive impact. The study highlights the importance of considering retaliatory measures in evaluating the effectiveness of protectionist trade policies.
